title: Labor targets ‘out of date’ Comcare scheme amid surge in work pressure claims
full_text:
Tailored, early support for injured workers to increase their capacity to return to work and a simpler process to improve management of claims will be the guiding principles behind reform of the federal workers compensation scheme, as the government seeks to address an almost threefold increase in claims attributed to work pressure.
In a speech on Wednesday, Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth will say the approach taken by Comcare is often out of date and piecemeal, resulting in injured workers being out of work longer than necessary.
Questioning whether the scheme’s governance settings are fit for purpose, Ms Rishworth will say Comcare does not have the same emphasis on early intervention as state schemes, and early support would get workers back to their jobs faster and avoid harm caused by lengthy claims.
“The longer someone is out of the workplace because of injury, the less likely they are to return to work,” she will say.
“Research indicates that if someone is off work because of injury for 20 days, the likelihood of that person returning to work is 70 per cent. But after 70 days away from the workplace, the likelihood that person returns to work drops dramatically, to just 35 per cent.”
The Comcare scheme covers more than 470,000 workers employed by the federal and ACT governments, and major national employers including Australia Post, Telstra, Commonwealth Bank, National Australia Bank and John Holland.
Data shows that psychological disease claims have grown strongly in recent years, driven by an almost threefold increase in claims attributed to work pressure. Psychological injuries are associated with poorer outcomes than physical claims, including more time out of work and lower return-to-work rates.
Based on current patterns, psychological claims are forecast to account for two-thirds of payments by 2029. For APS agencies, return-to-work rates for psychological claims are just 54 per cent compared to 91 per cent for physical injury claims.
Criticising Comcare as “broken, slow and almost 40 years out of date”, the ACTU says workers covered by it have fewer rights and weaker protections than those under state and territory schemes, and experience long delays, lost income, barriers to medical treatment, and little support to stay connected to their job.
The ACTU wants the government to adopt all 124 recommendations of an independent review of the Safety Rehabilitation and Compensation Act, which oversees the scheme, and to legislate to provide better protections and support to injured workers.
The review’s recommendations included requiring employers to provide safe, supported return-to-work plans, faster resolution of disputes, changing the practice of employers managing their own workers’ claims, and restoring legal rights for seriously injured workers to take action against negligent employers.
Ms Rishworth will say on Wednesday many workers compensation schemes have moved away from a process-driven approach to a person-centred approach, and shifted their priority to supporting workers safely return to health and employment.
“However, Comcare’s legislative framework and scheme design has not evolved in response to these contemporary approaches,” she will say. “Modern practices, like early intervention and tailored support to return to work, have not been adopted in a consistent way across the scheme.
“And this piecemeal approach means we are too often seeing injured workers remaining out of work longer than necessary. That is why our government is considering targeted reforms to ensure the scheme can continue to effectively deliver on its core functions and is sustainable into the future.”
Outlining four key reform principles, Ms Rishworth will say while improving prompt support for injured workers should be at the heart of any worker’s compensation scheme, the Comcare legislation and framework does not have the same emphasis on early support and intervention as other comparable schemes.
“I want to ensure that injured workers get appropriate support as early as possible, with a focus on recovery and maintaining a close connection with work,” she will say. “There is clear evidence that early support is critical to the recovery and return to work for injured workers. And timely support also reduces the potential additional harms that can be caused by lengthy claims processes.”
In seeking to ensure the rehabilitation and recovery process for workers is ultimately focused on supporting them to safely return to work, she will say return to work outcomes can be improved by employer-supported interventions that take a tailored and proactive approach to enabling injured workers to re-enter the workforce, whether through modified duties or finding suitable alternative employment.
“Compared to Comcare, other state-based schemes set clearer expectations for employers to support safe and sustainable return-to-work outcomes,” she will say.
“I think there is an opportunity to strengthen these arrangements within Comcare, and I will be looking at all levers to ensure that employer engagement in return-to-work processes is recognised as a core component of achieving better outcomes for injured workers.”
Identifying the need to modernise the scheme’s claims process, she will say she has heard from many people that its current design “makes the claims process challenging to navigate and overly focused on administrative processes at the expense of providing timely support”.
“As minister, I want to see fast and efficient management of claims so that both workers and employers can focus on recovery and a safe return to work rather than wrestling with paperwork,” she will say.
“And I am keen to explore ways we can make the claims process more user-friendly.”
The government is examining how to improve the scheme’s oversight and governance, including how to improve Comcare’s ability to engage with key stakeholders at a strategic level to help identify emerging trends and challenges, and making the allocation of return-to-work responsibilities between employers and rehabilitation authorities much clearer.
